title: The Hydraulic Press
statement:
A hydraulic press is a device for delivering very large forces. A conceptual sketch is shown below: two vertical pistons of different sizes are connected by a chamber full of fluid. The radius of the left piston is $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and the radius of the right piston is $$20\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The tops of the two pistons are at the same height. A truck of mass $$1500\;\mathrm{kg}$$ rests on the right piston. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

The press works because of the fluid's __pressure__. The basic equation relating pressure to force is $$P = \dfrac{F}{A},$$ or $$F = P\cdot A$$: the force applied by a fluid is its pressure times the area over which the force is applied.

__(a)__ A basic principle of fluid statics says: if there are no external forces on a stationary fluid, the pressure is the same everywhere in it. Justify this principle by considering a small cube of fluid somewhere in the middle of the chamber. (In this press, gravity does act on the fluid, so the pressure is actually slightly higher lower down — but since the tops of the two pistons are at the same height, we can safely ignore gravity's effect here.)

__(b)__ How much force $$F_L$$ must be applied downward on the left piston in order to support the truck? Before calculating, guess: does it take more or less than the truck's weight?

__(c)__ A small force lifting a heavy truck sounds too good to be true — what's the trade-off? If the left piston is pushed down a distance $$\Delta x_L,$$ how far $$\Delta x_R$$ does the truck rise? Answer using the work formula $$W = F\,\Delta x,$$ then show that your result is equivalent to a conservation law for the fluid. Conservation of what?

A more realistic hydraulic lift, shown below, adds at least one valve, so the small piston can be pumped back and forth many times without lowering the load — as you'll find in part (c), each pump raises the platform only a small amount.
answer: (b) $$F_L = 37.5\;\mathrm{N}$$; (c) $$\Delta x_R = \dfrac{\Delta x_L}{400}$$ — conservation of the fluid's volume.
solution:
__(a)__ Take a small cube of fluid in the middle of the chamber. If the pressure were different on one side of the cube than the other, the pressure forces on the cube's faces wouldn't cancel and there would be a net force on the cube. But the fluid is stationary — the cube isn't accelerating — so the net force on it is zero, and the pressure must be the same everywhere. (This is analogous to tension being constant along a massless rope, except the force is spread out over a surface instead of carried by a string.)

__(b)__ The right piston supports the truck, so the fluid pushes up on it with $$F_R = mg = 15\,000\;\mathrm{N}.$$ Since the pressure is the same at both pistons, $$P = \dfrac{F_R}{A_R} = \dfrac{F_L}{A_L},$$ giving $$F_L = \dfrac{F_R A_L}{A_R}.$$ The ratio of areas is the __square__ of the ratio of radii, $$\dfrac{A_R}{A_L} = \left(\dfrac{20}{1}\right)^2 = 400.$$ So $$F_L = \dfrac{15\,000\;\mathrm{N}}{400} = 37.5\;\mathrm{N}$$ — far less than the truck's weight. (If you got $$750\;\mathrm{N},$$ remember the area goes as the square of the radius; if you got $$3.75\;\mathrm{N},$$ don't forget $$g.$$)

__(c)__ The press cannot create energy, so the work done on the left equals the work done on the right: $$F_L\,\Delta x_L = F_R\,\Delta x_R,$$ or $$\Delta x_R = \dfrac{F_L}{F_R}\Delta x_L = \dfrac{\Delta x_L}{400}.$$ Comparing with the force equation from part (b), $$\dfrac{\Delta x_R}{\Delta x_L} = \dfrac{A_L}{A_R}.$$ Multiplying both sides by $$\Delta x_L\,A_R$$ gives $$\Delta x_R\,A_R = \Delta x_L\,A_L$$ — the volume of fluid pushed out of the left piston equals the volume pushed into the right piston. The trade-off is __conservation of volume__: we gain a factor of $$400$$ in force but lose the same factor of $$400$$ in distance.

title: The Hemispheres of Magdeburg
statement:
Otto von Guericke invented the vacuum pump in 1650. A few years later, he staged a dramatic demonstration to show the device off. He placed two hollow copper hemispheres in contact, then used the vacuum pump to suck most of the air out from between them. Next, von Guericke had two teams of eight horses each try to pull the hemispheres apart — and they couldn't.

Estimate the minimum radius of the hemispheres. Atmospheric pressure is approximately $$10^5\;\mathrm{Pa},$$ where the __pascal__ is the unit of pressure, $$1\;\mathrm{Pa} = 1\;\mathrm{N/m^2}.$$ Assume the mass of a horse is $$m = 500\;\mathrm{kg},$$ its coefficient of friction with the ground is $$\mu = 0.5,$$ and $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ The force from a fluid at pressure $$P$$ on a flat surface of area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(a)__ First, the concept: why do the evacuated hemispheres stick together at all? And if air had been allowed to freely enter the gap, would they still stick?

__(b)__ Estimate the maximum force one team of eight horses can exert. (Careful: a horse's pulling force is not its weight $$mg.$$ What actually limits how hard a horse can pull?)

__(c)__ To balance that pull, the atmosphere must push the hemispheres together hard enough. A tempting move is to compute the force on one hemisphere as the pressure times the hemisphere's curved surface area, $$F \stackrel{?}{=} P_0 \cdot \dfrac12\, 4\pi r^2.$$ Explain why that is wrong. Then find the correct net horizontal force from the atmosphere on one hemisphere, using this trick: imagine the hemisphere with its open end covered by a flat sheet, sitting in a uniform atmosphere — what must the net force on it be?

__(d)__ Estimate the minimum radius of the hemispheres.
answer: (b) $$F \approx 20\,000\;\mathrm{N}$$; (c) $$F = P_0 \pi r^2$$ — half the naive surface-area answer; (d) $$r \gtrsim 25\;\mathrm{cm}.$$
solution:
__(a)__ With a vacuum inside, the outside air pushes inward on each hemisphere with nothing pushing back from within, so a large net pressure force presses the two halves together; the normal force between them measures how tightly they're stuck. If air freely enters the gap, the inside air pushes outward and essentially cancels the inward push of the atmosphere, so the normal force drops to zero and the halves come apart easily. (Atmospheric pressure is enormous — it's the weight of roughly ten kilometers' worth of sea-level-density air above us — but we don't notice it because the pressure inside our bodies matches it.)

__(b)__ A horse pulls by pushing backward on the ground with friction, so its pull is limited by friction, not by its weight: $$F_h \approx \mu m g = 0.5 \cdot 500\;\mathrm{kg}\cdot 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2} = 2500\;\mathrm{N}$$ per horse, assuming each horse pulls so hard its hooves are about to slip. The team of eight exerts $$F = 8 F_h = 20\,000\;\mathrm{N}.$$ (Only one team's force matters: the other team just plays the role of an anchor, like a wall.)

__(c)__ The surface-area calculation is wrong because the pressure force is perpendicular to the surface everywhere, so on a curved hemisphere it points partly up in some places and partly down in others; those components cancel, and not all of the force points along the pulling direction. The trick: cover the open end with a flat sheet and place the object in a uniform atmosphere. It clearly feels zero net force, so the force on the curved part must exactly cancel the force on the flat disk, which is simply $$F = P_0 A = P_0 \pi r^2.$$ Therefore the net horizontal force on the curved hemisphere is $$P_0 \pi r^2$$ — exactly half the naive surface-area answer.

__(d)__ For the horses to fail, the pressure force must exceed the team's pull: $$\pi r^2 P_0 > N \mu m g$$ with $$N = 8.$$ Solving, $$r > \sqrt{\dfrac{20\,000\;\mathrm{N}}{\pi \cdot 10^5\;\mathrm{Pa}}} \approx 0.25\;\mathrm{m},$$ so the hemispheres needed a radius of at least about $$25\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The original hemispheres survive in the Deutsches Museum in Munich (photo below), and they're roughly the size of a large textbook — so the estimate is not bad: a sphere that small really can defeat a team of horses.

title: Pressure beneath the Surface of a Fluid
statement:
A vertical piston of cross-sectional area $$A$$ contains fluid of density $$\rho.$$ The atmosphere above the fluid has pressure $$P_0.$$ We insert a thin massless plate into the piston a distance $$h$$ beneath the surface of the fluid, as shown.

__(a)__ What is the mass of the column of fluid above the plate, in terms of $$\rho,$$ $$A,$$ and $$h?$$

__(b)__ List all the downward forces on the column of fluid above the plate, and find the upward force $$F$$ we must exert on the plate in order to hold up that column of fluid (with zero acceleration). The force from a fluid at pressure $$P$$ acting on area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(c)__ Now focus on the plate itself: it is pushed down by the fluid's pressure $$P$$ at depth $$h$$ and held up by the force $$F$$ you found. Use this to derive the formula for the pressure at depth $$h$$ below the surface of a fluid, as a function of $$\rho,$$ $$g,$$ $$h,$$ and $$P_0.$$

(This derivation assumes the density $$\rho$$ is constant — an excellent assumption for liquids like water, which barely compress under everyday pressures, but a poor one for a tall column of air, whose density thins out with height. On the F=ma exam, assume fluids have constant density and that this formula applies unless the problem says otherwise.)
answer: (a) $$m = \rho A h$$; (b) $$F = P_0 A + \rho g h A$$; (c) $$P = P_0 + \rho g h.$$
solution:
__(a)__ The volume of the column is base area times height, $$V = A h.$$ Mass is density times volume, so $$m = \rho V = \rho A h.$$

__(b)__ Two downward forces act on the column: gravity, $$F_g = mg = \rho A h g,$$ and the atmosphere pushing down on the top surface, $$F_P = P_0 A.$$ To hold the column with zero acceleration, our upward force must balance both: $$F = P_0 A + \rho A h g.$$

__(c)__ The plate is in equilibrium: the fluid just above it pushes down with force $$P A,$$ where $$P$$ is the fluid pressure at depth $$h,$$ and we push up with $$F.$$ Equating, $$PA = P_0 A + \rho g h A.$$ Dividing by $$A$$ gives the pressure-depth formula: $$P = P_0 + \rho g h.$$ Equivalently, pressure rises by $$\rho g\,\Delta y$$ for every distance $$\Delta y$$ you descend in the fluid.

title: Ranking the Forces on Three Flask Bottoms
statement:
Flasks $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C$$ each have a circular base with a radius of $$2\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ Flask $$A$$ has straight vertical walls, flask $$B$$ widens toward the top, and flask $$C$$ narrows toward the top, as sketched below. An equal volume of water is poured into each flask, and none overflow. (From the 2017 F=ma exam.)

Useful facts: the pressure at depth $$h$$ below the surface of water of density $$\rho$$ is $$P = P_0 + \rho g h,$$ where $$P_0$$ is atmospheric pressure, and the force from pressure $$P$$ on a flat area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(a)__ Rank the forces $$F_A,$$ $$F_B,$$ and $$F_C$$ exerted by the water on the bases of flasks $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C,$$ from greatest to least.

__(b)__ Here is an argument that the ranking should be a three-way tie: "Each flask holds the same volume — and hence the same weight — of water. That weight must be supported by the upward force from the flask's bottom, so the upward forces are equal, and by Newton's third law the forces from water on the three bases are equal too." The conclusion contradicts part (a). What does this argument miss? (Hint: it has nothing to do with the atmosphere; the same resolution would work in vacuum.)

__(c)__ Now compare an hourglass-shaped flask to a straight-walled flask with the same base, each holding the same volume of water (just enough to fill the hourglass's lower bulb and waist region). The hourglass has walls that slope inward lower down and outward higher up. Which flask's bottom feels the greater force from the water? And why don't the downward wall forces from the lower (inward-sloping) walls simply cancel the upward wall forces from the upper (outward-sloping) walls?
answer: (a) $$F_C > F_A > F_B$$; (b) it ignores vertical pressure forces from the slanted walls; (c) the hourglass — deeper water and stronger forces on the lower walls.
solution:
__(a)__ The force on each base is $$F = P\cdot A,$$ and the base areas are identical, so the ranking is decided by the pressure $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$ at the bottom — that is, by the water depth $$h.$$ With equal volumes, the narrowest flask has the deepest water: flask $$C$$ is narrowest on average, so its water is deepest; flask $$B$$ is widest, so its water is shallowest. Hence $$F_C > F_A > F_B.$$ (The tempting wrong answer $$F_B > F_A > F_C$$ comes from ranking by the area of the water's top surface, which is irrelevant to the force on the bottom.)

__(b)__ The argument forgets the vertical components of the pressure forces from the slanted side walls. In flask $$C,$$ the inward-leaning walls push down on the water (pressure forces are perpendicular to the wall), so the bottom must push up with more than the water's weight — and by Newton's third law the water pushes on the base with more than its weight. In flask $$B,$$ the outward-leaning walls push up on the water, so the bottom supports less than the water's weight. Only in straight-walled flask $$A$$ does the base force equal the water's weight exactly.

__(c)__ The hourglass is narrower on average than the straight flask, so the same volume of water stands deeper in it; the pressure at the bottom, $$P_0 + \rho g h,$$ is higher, and the force on the hourglass's bottom is greater. The wall forces don't cancel because pressure increases with depth: the lower, inward-sloping walls sit where the pressure is high and push down hard, while the upper, outward-sloping walls sit where the pressure is lower and push up more weakly. The net wall force is downward, which is exactly what the extra force on the bottom balances.

title: Gauge Pressure in a Plugged Milk Jug
statement:
The handle of a gallon of milk is plugged by a manufacturing defect. After removing the cap and pouring out some milk, the level of milk in the main part of the jug is lower than in the handle, as shown in the figure: the milk stands at height $$h$$ in the handle and at height $$H$$ in the main body, with $$h > H.$$ The main body is open to the atmosphere (pressure $$P_0$$); a pocket of trapped air sits at the top of the handle. The density of milk is $$\rho.$$ (From the 2017 F=ma exam.)

The __gauge pressure__ is the pressure minus atmospheric pressure: $$P_{\rm gauge} = P_{\rm abs} - P_0.$$ Recall that pressure in a fluid of constant density changes with height as $$\rho g \,\Delta y.$$

__(a)__ Which statement is true of the gauge pressure $$P$$ of the milk at the bottom of the jug? (a) $$P = \rho g h$$; (b) $$P = \rho g H$$; (c) $$\rho g H < P < \rho g h$$; (d) $$P > \rho g h$$; (e) $$P < \rho g H.$$ The key question: which height, $$h$$ or $$H,$$ is the relevant one, and why?

__(b)__ Find the pressure $$P_{\rm pocket}$$ of the trapped air pocket at the top of the handle, in terms of $$P_0,$$ $$\rho,$$ $$g,$$ $$h,$$ and $$H.$$ Is it higher or lower than atmospheric pressure?
answer: (a) choice (b): $$P = \rho g H$$; (b) $$P_{\rm pocket} = P_0 - \rho g (h - H),$$ which is below atmospheric pressure.
solution:
__(a)__ The answer is __(b)__. The surface of the milk in the main body is open to the atmosphere, so the pressure there is exactly $$P_0.$$ Descending a height $$H$$ from that surface to the bottom adds $$\rho g H,$$ so the absolute pressure at the bottom is $$P_{\rm abs} = P_0 + \rho g H,$$ and the gauge pressure is $$P = P_{\rm abs} - P_0 = \rho g H.$$ The column in the handle doesn't matter for the bottom: its surface is not at atmospheric pressure, because the plugged handle traps an air pocket whose pressure adjusts to whatever makes the milk levels consistent.

__(b)__ Measuring down from the pocket through the handle's milk column, the same bottom pressure must result: $$P_{\rm abs} = P_{\rm pocket} + \rho g h.$$ Setting the two expressions equal, $$P_0 + \rho g H = P_{\rm pocket} + \rho g h,$$ so $$P_{\rm pocket} = P_0 - \rho g (h - H).$$ Since $$h > H,$$ the pocket is at __less__ than atmospheric pressure — that's what holds the handle's milk up higher than the main body's. Equivalently: pressure falls by $$\rho g\,\Delta y$$ as you rise, and the pocket sits a height $$h - H$$ above the open surface, where the pressure is $$P_0.$$

title: The Bell That Lifts Itself
statement:
Water is poured through an orifice at the top into a hemispheric bell of radius $$R$$ lying on a table, tightly pressed against its surface. When the water level reaches the orifice — so the hemispherical space under the bell, of volume $$\dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac43 \pi R^3 = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi R^3,$$ is completely full — the bell lifts up and the water begins to flow out from underneath. Find the bell's mass $$M,$$ given that the density of water is $$\rho.$$ (From __Quantum__ magazine: Buzdin and Krotov, "Boy-oh-buoyancy," 1990.)

Useful facts: the (gauge) pressure at depth $$d$$ below the surface of water is $$\rho g d$$; the force from pressure $$P$$ on a flat area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$ You may ignore atmospheric pressure throughout, since the atmosphere pushes on everything evenly.

__(a)__ The bell lifts because the water's pressure pushes outward — and partly upward — on the bell's curved inner surface. Explain why computing that upward force directly is hard.

__(b)__ Find instead the downward pressure force from the water on the circle of table beneath the bell (radius $$R$$).

__(c)__ The force from part (b) is not the bell's weight — there's more work to do. Use Newton's third law and a force balance on the __water__ to find the net downward force the bell exerts on the water.

__(d)__ At the moment the bell is about to lift off, what supports the bell? Find the bell's mass $$M.$$
solution:
__(a)__ Two complications: the pressure varies from place to place on the bell (it grows with depth as $$\rho g d$$), and the pressure force is perpendicular to the curved surface, so it points in a different direction everywhere — only part of it points up. Adding it all up directly is a multivariable calculus problem. As with the Magdeburg hemispheres, we need a trick to avoid integrating over the curved surface.

__(b)__ The water touching the table is all at the same depth $$R,$$ where the gauge pressure is $$P = \rho g R,$$ and the force on the table is straight down. So $$F_{W\to T} = P \cdot A = \rho g R \cdot \pi R^2 = \pi \rho g R^3.$$

__(c)__ By Newton's third law, the table pushes up on the water with the same magnitude, $$\pi \rho g R^3.$$ The water is in equilibrium, so the upward force from the table balances the two downward forces on the water: gravity, $$\rho g \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}\pi R^3,$$ and the downward force from the bell on the water, $$F_{B\to W}.$$ Thus $$\pi \rho g R^3 = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi \rho g R^3 + F_{B \to W},$$ giving $$F_{B\to W} = \dfrac{\pi \rho g R^3}{3}.$$

__(d)__ By Newton's third law again, the water pushes up on the bell with $$\dfrac{\pi \rho g R^3}{3}.$$ At the moment of lift-off the table no longer presses on the bell, so this upward force alone supports the bell's weight: $$Mg = \dfrac{\pi \rho g R^3}{3},$$ so $$M = \dfrac{\pi \rho R^3}{3}.$$

title: Deriving the Buoyant Force
statement:
A cube with side length $$s$$ sits fully immersed in water of density $$\rho,$$ with its top face horizontal a distance $$h$$ below the surface, as shown. Gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ In this problem we derive, step by step, the net force that the water's pressure exerts on the cube. Recall that the pressure at depth $$d$$ below the surface is $$P = P_0 + \rho g d,$$ where $$P_0$$ is atmospheric pressure, and the force from pressure $$P$$ on a flat face of area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(a)__ The water pushes inward on all six faces of the cube. Do these pressure forces sum to zero? If not, which way does the net force point, and why?

__(b)__ Compute the pressure force on the top face and on the bottom face of the cube, and find the magnitude of the net pressure force on the cube. (The forces on the four side faces cancel in pairs.)

__(c)__ Rewrite your answer in terms of the cube's volume $$V.$$ This net pressure force is called the __buoyant force__. State the general principle — __Archimedes' principle__ — that your formula illustrates.

__(d)__ A student analyzing a beach ball held under the ocean draws a free-body diagram showing the pressure forces pushing inward on all sides of the ball __and__ an upward buoyant force $$F_B.$$ What is wrong with that diagram?
answer: (a) no — net force is upward; (b) $$F_B = \rho g s^3$$; (c) $$F_B = \rho g V$$ — the weight of the displaced fluid; (d) it double-counts: the buoyant force __is__ the sum of the pressure forces.
solution:
__(a)__ No. Pressure increases with depth, so the upward push on the cube's bottom face is stronger than the downward push on its top face (the side forces cancel by symmetry). The net pressure force points __up__.

__(b)__ The top face, at depth $$h,$$ feels a downward force $$F_{\rm top} = s^2\left(P_0 + \rho g h\right).$$ The bottom face is a distance $$s$$ lower, at depth $$h + s,$$ and feels an upward force $$F_{\rm bottom} = s^2\left(P_0 + \rho g (h+s)\right).$$ The net upward force is $$F_B = F_{\rm bottom} - F_{\rm top} = \rho g s^3.$$ Equivalently: the pressure on the bottom exceeds the pressure on the top by $$\Delta P = \rho g s,$$ and multiplying by the face area $$s^2$$ gives $$F_B = \rho g s^3.$$ Notice that both $$P_0$$ and the depth $$h$$ cancel — the buoyant force doesn't depend on how deep the cube sits.

__(c)__ Since $$s^3 = V,$$ we have $$F_B = \rho g V.$$ This is __Archimedes' principle__: a submerged object feels an upward buoyant force whose magnitude is the weight of the fluid it displaces — the fluid's density, times $$g,$$ times the displaced volume. (For a partially submerged object, $$V$$ is just the submerged volume.) Though we derived it for a cube, it holds for any shape.

__(d)__ The diagram double-counts. The buoyant force is not a separate force in addition to the pressure forces — it __is__ the net result of adding up all the pressure forces. In a calculation, use one description or the other: either sum the pressure forces directly, or use the buoyant force as a shortcut for that sum — never both.

title: The Pivoted Floating Rod
statement:
A uniform rod is partially in water with one end suspended from a pivot above the surface, as shown in the figure. The density of the rod is $$\dfrac{5}{9}$$ that of water. At equilibrium, what portion of the rod is above water? (From the 2013 F=ma exam.)

Treat the rod as very thin compared to its length $$\ell$$ (ignore the extra bits submerged because the rod is tilted). Let the rod have mass $$m$$ and uniform cross-sectional area $$A,$$ let a fraction $$\alpha$$ of its length be above the water, and let the rod make angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. Recall the buoyant force on an object has magnitude $$F_B = \rho_w g V_{\rm sub},$$ where $$\rho_w$$ is the water's density and $$V_{\rm sub}$$ the submerged volume, and that it points straight up.

__(a)__ This is a statics problem: the net force and the net torque on the rod must both be zero. Knowing the buoyant force's magnitude and direction isn't enough here — we also need to know __where__ it acts. The buoyant force can be modeled as acting at a single point called the __center of buoyancy__: the geometric center of the submerged part of the object (just as gravity acts at the center of mass). For our rod, how far from the pivot, measured along the rod, is the center of buoyancy? Is the center of buoyancy of an object always at the same place on the object?

__(b)__ Find the buoyant force on the rod in terms of $$m,$$ $$g,$$ and $$\alpha.$$ (First express the displaced mass using $$\rho_w,$$ $$A,$$ $$\ell,$$ and $$\alpha,$$ then eliminate $$\rho_w$$ using the given density ratio.)

__(c)__ Balance torques about the pivot to find $$\alpha.$$

__(d)__ If the rod were not pivoted but simply floated freely in the water, what fraction would be above the surface? Explain why the pivoted rod has more of its length above water than the free-floating rod.
answer: (c) $$\alpha = \dfrac{2}{3}$$ of the rod is above water; (d) $$\dfrac{4}{9}$$ if floating freely.
solution:
__(a)__ The submerged part is the lower section of length $$\ell(1-\alpha),$$ so its geometric center is a distance $$\alpha \ell + \dfrac12 \ell (1-\alpha) = \dfrac12 \ell (1+\alpha)$$ from the pivot, measured along the rod. No — unlike the center of mass, which is fixed by the object alone, the center of buoyancy depends on which parts of the object happen to be submerged: fully submerged, the rod's center of buoyancy is at its middle; half submerged, it is a quarter of the rod's length from the lower end.

__(b)__ The displaced volume is $$A\ell(1-\alpha),$$ so the displaced mass is $$m_{\rm dis} = \rho_w A \ell (1-\alpha).$$ Since the rod's density is $$\dfrac{m}{A\ell} = \dfrac{5}{9}\rho_w,$$ we have $$\rho_w = \dfrac{9}{5}\dfrac{m}{A\ell},$$ so $$m_{\rm dis} = \dfrac{9}{5}m(1-\alpha)$$ and $$F_B = m_{\rm dis}\,g = \dfrac{9}{5}mg(1-\alpha).$$

__(c)__ Take torques about the pivot, so the pivot force contributes nothing. The buoyant force acts at the center of buoyancy, whose horizontal moment arm is $$\dfrac12 \ell (1+\alpha)\cos\theta,$$ giving $$\tau_B = \dfrac{9}{5}mg(1-\alpha)\cdot\dfrac12 \ell (1+\alpha)\cos\theta = \dfrac{9}{10}\ell m g (1-\alpha^2)\cos\theta.$$ Gravity acts at the rod's center, with moment arm $$\dfrac12 \ell\cos\theta,$$ giving $$\tau_g = \dfrac12 \ell m g \cos\theta.$$ Setting $$\tau_B = \tau_g,$$ the factors $$\ell,$$ $$m,$$ $$g,$$ and $$\cos\theta$$ all cancel: $$\dfrac{9}{10}(1-\alpha^2) = \dfrac12,$$ so $$\alpha^2 = \dfrac49$$ and $$\alpha = \dfrac23.$$ Two thirds of the rod is above the water.

__(d)__ A freely floating object displaces its own weight of water, so the rod would need $$\dfrac59$$ of its volume submerged (the ratio of its density to water's), leaving $$\dfrac49$$ above the surface. The pivoted rod has __more__ above water ($$\dfrac23 > \dfrac49$$) because the pivot supplies part of the rod's support, so less buoyant force — hence less submerged volume — is needed.

title: How Much Does a Cable Stretch?
statement:
Any solid object deforms a little when forces act on it — every material behaves like a very stiff spring. In this problem we build up, by pure proportional reasoning, the law governing how much a cable stretches. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

A cable $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, of negligible weight, supports a hanging mass of $$100\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and stretches by $$0.5\;\mathrm{mm}.$$

__(a)__ How much would the same cable stretch if it supported $$200\;\mathrm{kg}$$ instead? (Materials under modest loads obey Hooke's law: stretch is proportional to the applied force.)

__(b)__ Keeping the $$200\;\mathrm{kg}$$ load, suppose the cable is replaced by one twice as long — $$2\;\mathrm{m}$$ — made of the same material with the same radius. What is the stretch now? (Hint: think of the $$2\;\mathrm{m}$$ cable as two $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ cables joined end to end.)

__(c)__ Keeping everything from part (b), now double the radius of the cable. What is the stretch? (Hint: think of the thick cable as several of the original cables banded together side by side.)

__(d)__ Keeping everything from part (c), replace the material with one twice as stiff — i.e. one that produces twice the tension for a given stretch. What is the stretch?

__(e)__ Combine the patterns from (a)-(d): a cable of length $$\ell$$ and cross-sectional area $$A,$$ made of a material whose stiffness is described by a single constant $$Y$$ (the __Young's modulus__), supports a load $$F.$$ Write the formula for the stretch $$\Delta \ell$$ (by convention, no extra numerical factor — that convention is what defines $$Y$$). Then rearrange the formula into the form $$\dfrac{F}{A} = Y\,\dfrac{\Delta \ell}{\ell},$$ and give the names and interpretations of the quantities $$\dfrac{F}{A}$$ and $$\dfrac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}.$$
solution:
__(a)__ Doubling the load doubles the tension (from $$1000\;\mathrm{N}$$ to $$2000\;\mathrm{N}$$), and by Hooke's law the stretch doubles: $$1\;\mathrm{mm}.$$

__(b)__ A $$2\;\mathrm{m}$$ cable is two $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ cables in series. Each carries the full tension of $$2000\;\mathrm{N},$$ so each stretches $$1\;\mathrm{mm},$$ for a total of $$2\;\mathrm{mm}.$$ Stretch is proportional to the cable's length.

__(c)__ Doubling the radius quadruples the cross-sectional area, so the thick cable acts like four original cables side by side. The load is shared four ways, each strand carries one quarter the tension, and the stretch drops by a factor of $$4$$ to $$0.5\;\mathrm{mm}.$$ Stretch is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

__(d)__ A material twice as stiff stretches half as much for the same force: $$0.25\;\mathrm{mm}.$$ Stretch is inversely proportional to the stiffness.

__(e)__ Stretch grows with the load $$F$$ and length $$\ell,$$ and shrinks with the area $$A$$ and stiffness $$Y$$: $$\Delta \ell = \dfrac{F\ell}{YA}.$$ Rearranged, $$\dfrac{F}{A} = Y\,\dfrac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}.$$ The quantity $$\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A}$$ is the __stress__ — force per unit area, like a pressure, but the word "stress" is used for solids. The quantity $$e = \dfrac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}$$ is the __strain__ — the fractional (percentage) increase in length. The relation $$\sigma = Y e$$ — stress equals Young's modulus times strain — is Hooke's law $$F = k\,\Delta x$$ adapted to describe materials in general: $$Y$$ characterizes the material itself, independent of the cable's dimensions. (Other deformations have their own moduli — compressing from all sides uses the strain $$\Delta V/V$$ and the "bulk modulus" — but so far only Young's modulus has appeared on the F=ma.)

title: The Tightrope Walker's Cable
statement:
A massless cable of diameter $$2.54\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is tied horizontally between two trees $$18.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ apart. A tightrope walker with a mass of $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ stands at the center of the cable. The cable stretches and makes an angle of $$1.50^\circ$$ with the horizontal. What is the cable's Young's modulus? Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Definitions you'll need: the __stress__ in a cable of tension $$T$$ and cross-sectional area $$A$$ is $$\sigma = \dfrac{T}{A}$$; the __strain__ is the fractional increase in length, $$e = \dfrac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}$$; and the __Young's modulus__ is their ratio, $$Y = \dfrac{\sigma}{e}.$$ Work through the following plan:

__(a)__ The walker hangs from two cable segments, one on each side, each with tension $$T$$ and each at $$1.50^\circ$$ below the horizontal. Find $$T.$$

__(b)__ Find the stress in the cable.

__(c)__ Find the strain: by what fraction is each segment longer than its unstretched (horizontal) length? (Hint: compare each segment's stretched length to the $$9.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ horizontal distance it spans.)

__(d)__ Combine your results to find the Young's modulus.
solution:
__(a)__ The walker is in equilibrium, so the vertical components of the two tensions support the weight: $$2T\sin\theta = mg,$$ giving $$T = \dfrac{80\cdot 10}{2\sin 1.50^\circ} \approx 1.53\times 10^4\;\mathrm{N}.$$ Notice how a small sag angle makes the tension huge compared to the walker's $$800\;\mathrm{N}$$ weight.

__(b)__ The cable's radius is $$1.27\;\mathrm{cm} = 0.0127\;\mathrm{m},$$ so $$A = \pi r^2 \approx 5.07\times 10^{-4}\;\mathrm{m^2}.$$ The stress is $$\sigma = \dfrac{T}{A} = \dfrac{mg}{2A\sin\theta} \approx 3.02\times 10^{7}\;\mathrm{Pa}.$$

__(c)__ Each segment spans a horizontal distance $$\ell = 9.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ and has stretched length $$\ell' = \dfrac{\ell}{\cos\theta},$$ since $$\ell = \ell'\cos\theta.$$ The strain is $$e = \dfrac{\ell'-\ell}{\ell} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - 1 \approx 3.43\times 10^{-4}.$$ (For small angles this is approximately $$\dfrac{\theta^2}{2}$$ with $$\theta$$ in radians: $$\theta = 0.0262\;\mathrm{rad}$$ gives $$3.43\times 10^{-4}.$$)

__(d)__ $$Y = \dfrac{\sigma}{e} = \dfrac{3.02\times 10^{7}\;\mathrm{Pa}}{3.43\times 10^{-4}} \approx 8.80\times 10^{10}\;\mathrm{Pa} = 88.0\;\mathrm{GPa}.$$ As a sanity check, that's a plausible stiffness for a real cable — steel is about $$200\;\mathrm{GPa},$$ and stranded or composite cables come out lower.
